records.summary: 270 Columbus Ave sits in the Broadway Neighborhood Commercial District (NCD-BROADWAY) where a Bar use on the first story and basement is a conditional use requiring Planning Commission approval. The site history shows continuous bar and restaurant operations since at least 2002, with a fast-food restaurant conditional use approved in 1985, followed by multiple approvals for full bar and full-service restaurant uses, and a Place of Entertainment permit approved in 2006. The block is extremely dense: 49 registered food and drink businesses within 500 ft (18 of them bars), 33 active on-sale ABC licenses within 500 ft, and 106 licenses within 1,000 ft, triggering ABC's undue-concentration flag.

comparables.key_takeaway: Planning approved live entertainment accessory to a bar at 253 Columbus (one door away), citing that bar is a permitted conditional use in Broadway NCD. As an agency referral, it shows Planning's willingness to support entertainment in existing bars on this block, though it does not test a full CUA hearing for a new bar use.

comparables.why_comparable: Restaurant with Place of Entertainment permit at 515 Broadway (34 m away, NCD-BROADWAY), an agency referral from 2021 approving nighttime entertainment accessory to an existing restaurant.
comparables.key_takeaway: Planning approved a POE permit for a restaurant on the same block in 2021, confirming that nighttime entertainment remains acceptable in NCD-BROADWAY when accessory to food service. This concept proposes entertainment as primary to a bar, which may require a full CUA hearing.

comparables.why_comparable: ABC Type 48 referral at 527 Broadway (23 m away, NCD-BROADWAY), approved 2019 for continuation of established bar use (Specs Twelve Adler Museum and Cafe).

comparables.why_comparable: CUA at 463–473 Broadway (112 m away, NCD-BROADWAY), filed 2001, approved to expand an existing bar from 2,500 to 4,300 square feet. This is a use decision showing Commission approval of bar expansion in the district.
comparables.key_takeaway: The Commission approved a bar expansion on Broadway in 2001, demonstrating that bar uses can be approved in NCD-BROADWAY when presented to the Commission. However, it was an expansion of an existing bar (not a change from restaurant to bar), and the approval was 21 years ago.

comparables.why_comparable: CUA at 493 Broadway (91 m away, NCD-BROADWAY), filed 2015, approved in 2016 to convert vacant adult entertainment and bar uses to a new restaurant with Other Entertainment use.
comparables.key_takeaway: The Commission approved a restaurant with entertainment use in 2016 on Broadway, showing willingness to support food-and-entertainment concepts in the district. The approval took 11 months (filed May 2015, decided April 2016), illustrating typical CUA timelines for entertainment uses.

comparables.why_comparable: CUA at 644 Broadway (145 m away, CCB district), filed 2016, approved in 2016 to change from movie theater to Other Entertainment (theater) with bar use for alcohol sales during performances.
comparables.key_takeaway: The Commission approved a bar use in conjunction with entertainment at a nearby venue, taking 5 months from filing to decision. This shows the Commission's openness to entertainment-plus-bar concepts in the immediate area, though CCB zoning is more permissive than NCD-BROADWAY.

comparables.why_comparable: Place of Entertainment agency referral at 1155 Grant (92 m away, CCB district), approved 2019 for POE accessory to an existing bar (Bow Wow Cocktail Lounge).
comparables.key_takeaway: Planning routinely approves POE permits as accessory to bars in the immediate neighborhood through agency referrals, but this is in CCB where bar use is permitted, not NCD-BROADWAY where bar requires conditional use.

patterns.pattern: Agency referrals on the Columbus/Broadway corridor consistently approve Place of Entertainment permits and Limited Live Performance permits as accessory uses to existing bars and restaurants, but these are staff-level approvals that do not test whether the Commission would approve a change of use from restaurant to bar at a public hearing.

Bars and entertainment venues in NCD-BROADWAY and adjacent CCB district have been approved by the Commission when presented as expansions of existing uses or as restaurant-plus-entertainment concepts, but the record contains only dated CUA approvals (2001, 2016) for bar-related uses in NCD-BROADWAY.

CUA timelines for entertainment and bar uses in this area range from 5 to 11 months from filing to decision, with no record of extended delays or denials for entertainment concepts in the recent decade.

risk.concept_summary: A 5,478 sq ft cocktail bar with full kitchen, live entertainment and amplified sound, 70 seats, serving full liquor and food, closing after midnight but before 2 a.m., at 270 Columbus Ave in the Broadway Neighborhood Commercial District.

overall.next_step: Confirm in writing with Planning whether the concept is part of a chain and whether storefronts will be merged, then file a Conditional Use Authorization application for bar use, preparing a neighborhood outreach plan and sound-mitigation strategy before the hearing.

approvals.summary: A Conditional Use Authorization hearing is required because bar use is a conditional use in NCD-BROADWAY, and formula retail and use size controls are not decided due to missing information on chain status and storefront merger.

findings.text: In the Broadway Neighborhood Commercial District, a bar on the first story and basement is a conditional use under Planning Code § 714, requiring Planning Commission approval.

The concept is a change of use from Restaurant to Bar and Nighttime Entertainment; the rules treat the last use as restaurant per the applicant's description, though no active ABC license is on file at 270 Columbus Ave.

Nighttime Entertainment on the first story and basement is principally permitted in NCD-BROADWAY under Planning Code § 714; the entertainment component itself does not require conditional use approval.

The concept's 5,478 sq ft exceeds the district's 3,000 sq ft use size threshold for conditional use, but Zoning Administrator Interpretation 121.2 may exempt a change of use within the same floor area if no significant expansion occurs and storefronts are not merged.
The rules could not decide whether formula retail or use size controls apply because the description does not state whether the business is part of a chain or whether storefronts will be merged.
N = 5 dated use decisions in NCD-BROADWAY within 1,000 ft over 10 years: 3 approved, 2 withdrawn, 0 denied, too few to calculate an approval rate.

approvals.summary: Insufficient information: the rules cannot determine which ABC licence process applies because the description does not state how the Type 48 license will be obtained (new application or transfer from another owner or location).

findings.text: The concept seeks an ABC Type 48 (on-sale general, public premises) license for a bar. State law limits Type 48 licenses by county population; San Francisco County exceeds its quota, so new licenses must be obtained by purchasing and transferring an existing license unless an exception applies.

Census tract 106.00 shows 52 active on-sale retail licenses as of March 16, 2022, against 12 authorized under ABC's census tract allocation, triggering an undue-concentration test under Business and Professions Code § 23958.4.

19 ABC licenses within 1,000 ft and 15 in the census tract were on file on March 16, 2022, but their status that day is unknown because ABC's daily reports show status changes since then; they are excluded from the concentration counts.

The description does not state how the Type 48 license will be obtained—whether by original application, person-to-person transfer, or premises-to-premises transfer—so the rules cannot apply the correct ABC review process or concentration test.

Comparable bars on the Columbus/Broadway corridor hold active Type 48 licenses: 256 Columbus (12 m away, issued 2014), 546 Broadway (40 m), 255 Columbus (49 m, issued 1965), demonstrating that Type 48 licenses operate in the immediate area.

approvals.summary: A Place of Entertainment permit hearing is required by the Entertainment Commission because the concept includes live entertainment with amplified sound as a primary use; nearby bars with entertainment have obtained POE permits through Commission hearings.

findings.text: Police Code § 1060 requires a Place of Entertainment permit for venues where live performance, DJs or amplified entertainment is a primary use; the Entertainment Commission holds a public hearing on each POE application.

Planning approved Limited Live Performance permits as accessory to existing bars at 253 Columbus (35 m away, approved 2018) and Place of Entertainment permits for restaurants with entertainment at 515 Broadway (34 m, approved 2021) in NCD-BROADWAY.

A POE permit was approved at 270 Columbus Ave in 2006 (filed June 21, decided same day) for a request covering Place of Entertainment and Extended Hours; the 2006 approval noted that Section 714.48 permits Other Entertainment uses on the first and second floors in Broadway NCD.

The POE application is sent to five departments for review: Police, Planning, Building Inspection, Public Health and Fire; the concept must post a 30-day notice at the premises and undergo a Commission hearing.

approvals.summary: A health permit to operate is allowed as of right after plan check and inspection; bars serving food need a health permit, which is issued without a hearing once the facility meets health code requirements.

findings.text: A food or drink business needs a health permit to operate under the California Retail Food Code and San Francisco Health Code Article 8; the permit is issued after plan check and pre-opening inspection, without a discretionary hearing.

The health permit application is referred to Planning for zoning review; a bar with a full kitchen needs both a plan check ($828–$2,207 for 2026–27) and a permit to operate ($470 application fee, $0 annual license fee for 2026–28).
Full-service restaurant and full-bar uses were last approved at 270 Columbus Ave in 2007 per agency referral MB0700727; earlier approvals in 2003 and 2004 also noted full kitchen and full bar.

approvals.summary: A building permit with change of use is required for the tenant improvements and the change from restaurant to bar; the permit must conform to the Planning Code (requiring the CUA approval first) before DBI will issue it.

findings.text: The concept is a change of use from Restaurant to Bar and Nighttime Entertainment under Planning Code § 102; San Francisco Building Code § 106A.1 requires a building permit for a change of use.

Planning Code § 175 requires that a building permit conform to the Planning Code before it is issued; the building permit will be routed to Planning for zoning review, and DBI will not issue the permit until the CUA is approved.

The existing occupancy group of the space is not in public records; only plans or an inspection establish it. A restaurant or bar for 50 or more occupants is Building Code Group A-2; the concept's 70 seats imply at least 50 occupants, so a change of occupancy is not established but is likely.

Tenant improvements are described in the concept; a bar build-out with sound and lighting systems for entertainment will need architectural plans, mechanical and electrical permits, and coordination with the health department's plan check.

expected_conditions.condition: Hours of operation limited to closing by 2 a.m. (no Extended Hours permit is sought; a nearby restaurant CUA was conditioned to close by 10 p.m. in 2019, but bar hours in NCD-BROADWAY are principally permitted until 2 a.m.).
expected_conditions.basis: Planning Code § 714 permits hours from 6 a.m. to 2 a.m. in NCD-BROADWAY without conditional use; the 2019 CUA at 279 Columbus Ave (41 m away) imposed a 10 p.m. closing condition on a restaurant, but comparable bar approvals in the district have not been conditioned below 2 a.m.

expected_conditions.condition: Security plan and good-neighbor policy: the Entertainment Commission and Police Department routinely condition POE permits to require security staffing (e.g., one guard for every 50–100 patrons), ID checks at the door, and a written good-neighbor policy addressing noise, smoking and loitering.
expected_conditions.basis: POE permits reviewed by Police include security and neighborhood-impact conditions as standard practice; the concept's 70-seat capacity and live entertainment will trigger these requirements.

expected_conditions.condition: Sound level limits and soundproofing: the POE permit will likely require that amplified sound not exceed a specified decibel level at the property line or at nearby residential units, and may condition approval on installation of soundproofing materials, a sound limiter on the PA system, or closing…
expected_conditions.basis: Entertainment Commission and Planning precedent for venues with live music in mixed-use neighborhoods; the 2016 CUA at 644 Broadway (145 m away) for a theater with bar included soundproofing conditions.

expected_conditions.condition: Alcohol service limited to Type 48 license terms: no minors on the premises, no sales after 2 a.m., and maintenance of a bona fide public-premises operation (ABC Type 48 does not require food service, but the concept includes a full kitchen).
expected_conditions.basis: ABC Type 48 licenses prohibit minors and limit sales hours to 2 a.m. under state law; the license is for a bar (public premises), not an eating place.

expected_conditions.condition: Neighborhood notification and outreach: the CUA will require a Section 311 notice mailed to properties within 300 feet and posted at the site for 30 days; the applicant should conduct pre-application outreach to neighbors and the North Beach Neighbors association.
expected_conditions.basis: A change of use to bar in an NC district requires Section 311 neighborhood notification under Planning Code § 311(b); early outreach is recommended practice for bar and entertainment CUAs to address concerns before the hearing.

expected_conditions.condition: Three-year vesting period: the CUA authorization is valid for three years, within which a building or site permit must be issued and construction commenced diligently to completion.
expected_conditions.basis: Standard CUA condition of approval in San Francisco; the 2019 CUA at 279 Columbus included this vesting language.

filing_playbook.action: Form the legal entity (California LLC or corporation) with the Secretary of State and obtain a federal EIN immediately.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: File Articles of Organization (LLC-1, $70) or Articles of Incorporation ($100) online at bizfile.sos.ca.gov; the entity name will appear on the lease, ABC license and all city permits. Apply for the EIN at irs.gov the same day (free, issued instantly Mon–Fri). Register for California seller's permit and EDD employer account within the first week.

filing_playbook.action: Register the business with San Francisco Treasurer & Tax Collector to obtain a Business Account Number (BAN); file a fictitious business name statement if the public-facing name differs from the legal entity name.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Complete the business registration online at sftreasurer.org using the EIN and entity documents; the $55–$95 registration fee (depending on projected gross receipts) gives you a BAN, which every other city department will ask for. If the bar will operate under a trade name, file the FBN statement with the County Clerk and publish it in a court-approved newspaper within 45 days.

filing_playbook.action: Request a pre-application meeting with SF Planning to confirm the zoning pathway, discuss the use size and formula retail questions, and outline the CUA timeline and requirements.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Email the Current Planning front desk (currentplanning@sfgov.org) with the address, concept description, square footage and the three open questions (chain status, storefront merger, license acquisition method). Ask Planning to confirm in writing whether the 3,000 sq ft use size control applies under Zoning Administrator Interpretation 121.2 if the floor area does not grow, and whether the concept is formula retail. Bring this confirmation to the CUA application.

filing_playbook.action: Engage an architect, acoustical consultant and kitchen/mechanical engineer to prepare preliminary plans and a sound-attenuation strategy before filing the CUA.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Commission an acoustic baseline study of the space and adjacent residential units, and design soundproofing measures (wall/ceiling insulation, vibration isolators, door seals, PA limiters) sufficient to meet Entertainment Commission standards. Have the architect prepare scaled floor plans showing the bar layout, seating, performance area, kitchen and restrooms, and the mechanical engineer assess the existing hood and grease interceptor. These documents support the CUA application and will be required for the building and health permits.

filing_playbook.action: Conduct neighborhood outreach: present the concept to the North Beach Neighbors association, meet with adjacent property owners and businesses, and document all outreach in writing.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Schedule a presentation at a North Beach Neighbors meeting (or meet with the board) at least one month before filing the CUA. Explain the concept, operating hours (closing by 2 a.m.), sound-mitigation plan, security staffing and good-neighbor commitments (e.g., no sidewalk queuing, no smoking in front, complaint hotline). Request a letter of support or neutrality. Walk door-to-door to businesses and residents within 300 feet, leave a one-page summary with contact information, and log every conversation. Attach this outreach log to the CUA application.

filing_playbook.action: File the Conditional Use Authorization application with SF Planning, paying the $3,100–$15,000 fee (depending on construction cost) and submitting the preliminary plans, acoustic report, neighborhood outreach log and project narrative.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: The project narrative should frame the concept as continuing a bar-and-entertainment tradition on this block (cite the 2006 POE approval at 270 Columbus, the 2018 LLP at 253 Columbus, and bar operations at 256 Columbus and 527 Broadway), demonstrate how the concept supports the Broadway NCD's nightlife character, commit to the sound-mitigation measures and good-neighbor policy, and confirm that hours will close by 2 a.m. without an Extended Hours permit. Request First Year Free fee waiver consideration if eligible. Planning will route the application to environmental review, schedule the Section 311 neighborhood notification, and calendar the Commission hearing (typically 4–6 months after filing).

filing_playbook.action: While the CUA is pending, engage a liquor license broker to identify and escrow an ABC Type 48 license for transfer to 270 Columbus Ave; submit the ABC transfer application only after the CUA is approved.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Because San Francisco County is over quota for Type 48 licenses, the license must be purchased from an existing holder and transferred. License brokers quote Type 48 prices at $100k–$450k in San Francisco (as of 2022); expect a 90–180 day transfer timeline once ABC receives the application. Make the purchase contract contingent on CUA and ABC approval. Do not file the ABC application until the CUA is granted, because ABC will ask Planning for a zoning referral and Planning will not approve the referral until the CUA motion is final (30 days after the Commission vote).

filing_playbook.action: After the Planning Commission approves the CUA (and the 30-day appeal period expires), file the ABC Type 48 transfer application, the Entertainment Commission Place of Entertainment permit application, and the building permit application concurrently.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: The ABC application requires the signed lease, entity documents, seller's permit, the CUA motion, and the escrowed license number; ABC will refer it to SF Police and SF Planning (Planning will issue a zoning referral approval citing the CUA). The POE application goes to the Entertainment Commission with the CUA approval, the acoustic report, the security and good-neighbor plans, and the $2,708 application fee; the Commission will post a 30-day notice and schedule a hearing. The building permit application (with stamped architectural plans) is submitted to DBI and routed to Planning, which will issue a Planning Department zoning referral approval citing the CUA and confirming the change of use.

filing_playbook.action: File the DPH plan check application for the kitchen and bar layout simultaneously with the building permit; schedule the DPH plan review meeting and address any comments before construction starts.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: Submit two sets of scaled floor plans, interior photos, the menu, and the equipment list through the DPH online portal (sfdph.org/ehsportal) with the $828–$2,207 plan check fee. The plan reviewer will confirm that the existing kitchen equipment, hood, grease interceptor and hand sinks meet health code requirements for the proposed use, or require upgrades. Obtain DPH plan approval before pulling the building permit, and coordinate a pre-final DPH inspection at 80% construction completion.

filing_playbook.action: Once DBI issues the building permit and construction is substantially complete, schedule final inspections with DBI, DPH and the Fire Department; obtain the Certificate of Final Completion, the health permit to operate and the Fire Department Place of Assembly permit before opening.
filing_playbook.what_to_say: The building permit final inspection confirms that the space matches the approved plans and meets code (ADA access, exits, restrooms, mechanical systems). The DPH pre-opening inspection (schedule two weeks in advance with your plan reviewer) checks that the kitchen is operational, a certified food safety manager is on staff, and the space meets the health code; DPH issues the permit to operate after this inspection passes. The Fire Department inspects occupant load signage and the hood suppression system and issues the Place of Assembly permit. All three permits must be posted on site before the public enters. Then await ABC's final premises inspection and the Entertainment Commission's POE hearing decision.

timeline_cost.notes: These figures are the time and government cost to obtain the four approvals in the entitlement path (Conditional Use Authorization, Place of Entertainment permit, Health permit to operate, and Building permit with change of use) when they are granted. The timeline runs from forming the entity to receiving all four approvals: 8.5–24 months. The cost range includes government fees only (CUA $3,100–$15,000; POE permit $2,708; health plan check $828–$2,207 and permit $470; building permit $800–$15,000; plus business registration $55–$700, state entity formation $70–$150, sellers permit $0, EDD registration $0, food safety manager $100–$250, RBS training $50–$360 for 12 staff, fire Place of Assembly $446, FOG program $0–$500, sign permit $300–$1,500, and music licenses $600–$5,000 per year); it does not include the cost of purchasing the ABC Type 48 license ($17,000 minimum for a newly released quota license, $100,000–$450,000 for a transferred license on the open market in San Francisco as of 2022), nor the 120–300 day ABC transfer timeline, nor any professional fees (architect, acoustical consultant, license broker, attorney). The timeline assumes the CUA is approved on first hearing (4–6 months after filing) and the POE permit is approved at the first Entertainment Commission hearing (3–4 months after CUA approval); the building permit and health permits follow construction and final inspections (2–6 months). A CUA denial, a continued hearing, or a discretionary review request would extend the timeline by 3–12 months. The timeline does not account for withdrawal, denial or cancellation; the decision times block shows that two of five dated NCD-BROADWAY bar/restaurant use decisions were withdrawn (no time to approval for those cases).
